name: Lower Düden Waterfalls
label: Lower Düden Falls
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Düden Parkı' (4 web pages); placed at our map tiles: 'Düden Park' (pois).
pin_note: Position set at the correction gate (pin check 2026-11-17: moved onto the OSM object with the sight's Wikidata ID).
notes: Waterfall dropping from the cliff into the Mediterranean.

text.description:
Here the Düden River drops 40 metres (131 ft) off the cliff into the Mediterranean. That mix of white water, rock and open sea is why it is the first photo most visitors take. The waterfall sits inside Düden Park, and the park's main viewing terrace on the cliff top gives a side-on view of the water leaving the cliff edge, with the sea right beside it. There is no walking route down to the base, so a head-on view from below is only possible from a boat. From the terrace the side view is the one to go for, and it is the classic Düden frame.

The cliff slope can tilt your picture, so turn on the gridlines and line the horizon up with one of them. Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) or the default lens (1x) to get the fall, the cliff and the sea in one frame. Then try a zoom (2x or more) to pick out just the falling water. Take a few shots at each setting, because the light changes quickly on the coast. If you have time, Gençlik Parkı is a second option: it gives a side view of the water crashing into the sea, framed by the park's greenery. Don't confuse this waterfall with Upper Düden, which is a separate, fenced site elsewhere in the province.
text.geographic_location: On Antalya's Mediterranean coast, inside Düden Park, where the Düden River drops over the cliff into the sea.
text.directions_text: No tram or railway stop is listed near the falls, so navigate to Düden Parkı on the coast. Once in the park, walk to the cliff-top viewing terrace on the side facing the sea. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) or the default lens (1x) to fit the falls, cliff edge and sea into one frame. Use a zoom lens (2x or more, depending on your phone) for a tighter shot of the falling water.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Düden Parkı (cliff-top main viewing terrace above the falls, on the side facing the sea). The falls dropping from the cliff edge into the sea, seen from the side, with the sea beside them. The falls lie to the south-west of you.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and put the horizon on a line, because the slope of the cliff can tilt the picture. Keep the falls on one side and the open sea on the other so the drop reads clearly. For another version of the shot, Gençlik Parkı gives a side view of the water crashing into the sea, framed by greenery.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the brightest water to focus, then lower the exposure slider a little so the white water keeps its detail. Try a Live Photo to catch the movement of the fall, and wipe your lens first if there is any spray.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Sunset is the time a photo guide recommends, because the light gives strong tones against the sea.

text.access_note: Düden Park is open to the public and free of charge, but check the official site before you go for current hours and any changes.

name: Konyaaltı Beach
label: Konyaaltı Beach
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Cam Piramit' (1 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Cam Piramit Sabancı Kongre ve Fuar Merkezi' (way/425188380): middle (93 m across); moved 35 m off buildings.
pin_note: Position from Wikidata Q2493895: kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.
notes: Long pebble beach backed by the Taurus Mountains.

text.description:
Konyaaltı Beach is one of Antalya's two main beaches, the other being Lara. It runs along the western side of the city for about 13 km, mostly fine pebbles with some sand, and it holds Blue Flag status for water quality. The beach park, bars, cafes and hotels sit along its inland edge, and the Aqualand waterpark on Dumlupınar Bulvarı marks the other end. Turkish pines and hibiscus grow along the front.

For photographs, the best idea is to go up rather than down to the shingle. The park and viewing terrace around the glass pyramid (Cam Piramit) give a wider, higher view than the shoreline. From there you see the curve of the beach, the green park areas, the coast stretching on toward Lara and the mountains in the distance. The glass pyramid also makes a handy landmark to put in the foreground. If you want the classic mountain-and-sea picture, the pebble shore with the Beydağları peaks behind is the other option. For a quieter shoreline view, try the eastern end of the beach near Dumlupınar Bulvarı.

Bring a lens cloth, as sea air can smear the glass. Keep the horizon level using the gridlines. Stay on the public walkways, because swimming and beach-club areas may limit where you can stand down on the sand.
text.geographic_location: Konyaaltı Beach is on the western side of Antalya, with the beach park and hotels along its inland edge.
text.directions_text: No public transport stop is listed for this spot; check a map app for how to reach the glass pyramid (Cam Piramit) park above Konyaaltı Beach. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to take in the park, the pyramid and the whole sweep of beach. Then switch to the default lens (1x) for a calmer, more natural view. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out the mountains or a stretch of coast.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand at Cam Piramit (park area and viewing terrace around the glass pyramid, Runtalya village). An elevated panorama over the beach, the park areas and the coastline stretching toward Lara, with the mountains in the distance. Konyaaltı Beach is to the south-west.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and put the horizon on the upper or lower line, depending on whether you want more sea or more beach. Use the glass pyramid or a park path as a foreground anchor. For a different view, go down to Konyaaltı Plajı for the pebble shore with the Beydağları peaks behind, or to the eastern end by Dumlupınar Bulvarı for a quieter stretch.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the mountains to set focus, then pull the exposure slider down a little so the sky keeps its colour. Try panorama mode for the full length of the coast, moving slowly and keeping the phone level.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light and clearer mountains than the middle of a summer day.

text.access_note: The terrace and park around the glass pyramid appear to be open public space, but beach clubs and swimming areas below may restrict access, so check the official site before you go.

name: Hadrian's Gate
label: Hadrian's Gate
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Atatürk Caddesi' (1 web pages); placed at the stretch of Atatürk Caddesi nearest the subject (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/91728341: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Hadrian's Gate' (29 m across).
notes: Triple-arched Roman gate at the entrance to Kaleiçi.

text.description:
Hadrian's Gate is a Roman memorial gate, built in honour of the emperor Hadrian, who visited the city in 130 CE. It has three arches, with a tower on each side. It is built of white marble, apart from the granite pillars, and is only about 8 metres high, so it feels close and easy to take in. The arches are decorated with flower and rosette carvings, and the top edge has a band of floral reliefs and a cornice with lion heads. The southern tower is Roman. The upper part of the northern tower was rebuilt in the 13th century and carries an Arabic inscription, so you can see two eras in one frame. Today it is the only surviving entrance gate in the old city walls. The walls hid it for years, which helped protect it. It was restored in 1959. Walk through the central arch and you can look down through a clear panel at the original Roman paving, with deep cart grooves worn into it.

It photographs well because the three arches make a natural frame, with the Old Town lanes opening up behind them. For the classic shot, take the straight-on view from Atatürk Caddesi so the arches sit symmetrically. Switch on gridlines to keep the pillars upright. Then step in close for the carvings and the floor panel. The gate sits on a busy boulevard, so wait for a gap in the traffic before you shoot.
text.geographic_location: Hadrian's Gate is in central Antalya, where the modern boulevard, Atatürk Caddesi, meets the walled Old Town. It stands in the old city wall and is the only entrance gate left there.
text.directions_text: There are no tram or railway stops nearby, so head on foot to the edge of the Old Town on Atatürk Caddesi and look for Hadrian's Gate (Üçkapılar). The gate stands where the boulevard meets the Old Town lanes. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the straight-on view of all three arches. Use ultra-wide (0.5x) if the boulevard is crowded and you cannot step back, but keep the gate centred so the edges do not stretch. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the lion-head cornice and the floral carvings.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Atatürk Caddesi (boulevard side, facing the gate from the modern-city end). A straight-on frontal view of the three arches with the Old Town lanes opening beyond them.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Centre the middle arch and use gridlines to keep the pillars upright. Wait for a gap in the traffic so the road does not cut across the base. For a different view, shoot from inside the Old Town looking back through the arches to the boulevard, or find a slightly raised spot with the boulevard fountain behind the gate. Guides disagree on which side is best, so try a couple of positions.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the marble to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the white stone keeps its detail and the arches do not look washed out. If the arches are dark against a bright sky, try the phone's HDR or auto-exposure setting. After dark, use night mode and hold the phone against a wall or railing to keep it steady.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: One guide suggests shooting from the western side in the morning, with the sun behind you, but that side is unconfirmed, so check the light when you arrive. The gate is also lit after dark, which makes a good night-mode shot.

text.access_note: The gate stands in an open public street and you can walk through it, but check the official site before you go if you plan to climb the tower or visit at a particular time.
claims_not_in_sources: The walled Old Town next to the gate is known as Kaleiçi.
The gate is lit after dark.
The boulevard in front of the gate is busy with traffic, so gaps are needed for clean shots.
Tapping to focus and lowering exposure helps keep detail in white marble.

label: Antalya Aquarium

text.description:
Antalya Aquarium is an attraction on this map, and it works well as a photo stop because you can treat the building as a landmark shot. Capture the whole entrance or façade first, then move closer for details such as signs, colours and shapes.

Switch on the gridlines and keep the building's vertical edges lined up with them so it doesn't lean. If people are walking in front of the entrance, wait a few seconds for a gap, or include them on purpose to show the scale of the place. Take one wide shot to show the setting and one closer one for the details.

Take several quick shots rather than one, then keep the sharpest.

Check the official site before you go for current rules and access arrangements.

text.directions_text: No rail or tram stops are listed for this spot. Follow the map to the phone icon on the map. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. Photograph the entrance and outer walls from where you stand, then step back if you can do so safely and need more of the building in the frame.

name: Antalya Museum
label: Antalya Museum
camera_source: No separate stand-here point: photographed at the spot itself (indoors, from its top, or right in front of it); drawn as the split pin.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/435948613: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Antalya Archeological Museum' (180 m across).
notes: Major archaeology museum with Perge statues.

text.description:
Antalya Museum, also called the Antalya Archaeological Museum, was one of Turkey's largest museums. It covers about 7,000 square metres, with 13 exhibition halls and an open-air gallery. It showed some 5,000 works that tell the story of the Mediterranean coast and the ancient region of Pamphylia. Its best-known displays were the Roman statues from Perge, including emperors and the administrator Plancia Magna, and a hall of carved sarcophagi. It was also the first Turkish museum building to come out of an architectural competition, held in 1964.

Please note that the museum is currently closed. Demolition began in 2025 and a new building is being planned, so you will be photographing a site in transition rather than the old galleries. That can still make an honest travel record: the long, low building outline (or what remains of it), any hoardings and the city around it. It is a different picture from the one earlier visitors took, so treat it as a quick stop rather than a destination. What you can see and reach may change from week to week, so check the official site before you go.

Keep your phone photos simple. Take one wide frame to show the scale of the site, then one or two closer shots of signs or details that tell the story. Look out for reflections on glass and for fencing in front of the lens.
text.geographic_location: The museum site is in the Muratpaşa district, in the urban part of Antalya. It is a large plot, roughly 180 metres across.
text.directions_text: No station or tram stop is listed for this spot, so start from the Muratpaşa area of central Antalya and go by taxi or hired scooter to the museum site. Once you are in the area, use the phone icon on the map as your target. Check the official site for the current state of the site before you set out. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to take in the width of the site. Use the default lens (1x) for a natural view of the building or hoardings. If you have a telephoto (2x-5x), use it for signs and details from a distance.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. If fencing or building works block the way, step back to the nearest open public spot and photograph from there. Do not go into any closed area.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and keep the horizon level so the long building line looks straight. Take one wide shot for context, then a second tighter one of a detail, such as a sign or the edge of the structure. Avoid shooting straight at glass or shiny barriers, as your phone will show up in the reflection.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the building to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly if the sky is bright, so the walls do not turn dark. Check that the photo is sharp before you move on.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light and fewer harsh shadows than midday. The site is under works, so it may be quieter outside working hours.

text.access_note: The museum is closed and the site is being rebuilt, so access may be restricted: check the official site before you go.

name: Karaalioğlu Park
label: Karaalioğlu Park
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Hıdırlık Kulesi' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Hıdırlık Kulesi' (way/110321832): middle (35 m across); moved 10 m off buildings.
pin_note: Position from OSM W110321827 (Karaalioğlu Parkı): kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.
notes: Clifftop park with sea and mountain views.

text.description: Karaalioğlu Park is a clifftop park on Antalya's coast, with gardens, fountains and sea views. The best picture of it comes from the cliff edge beside Hıdırlık Tower. The tower makes a strong foreground, and behind it the cliff edge, the sea and the coastline open out into a wide panorama. Photo guides call the cliffs near the tower the best panoramic spot in the park. The tower has a Roman-era backstory, which adds interest to the shot. Check on the day whether the tower sits at the west or the south end of the park, and use the tower itself as your landmark rather than the compass. If you want a second angle, the park's sea-facing terrace (Karaalioğlu Parkı Seyir Terası) looks out over the bay and harbour. The Dancing Girls statue (Dans Eden Kızlar Heykeli) shows the inside of the park, with gardens and fountains instead of sea. Start with the wide view at the tower, then walk into the park for the quieter garden scenes. Keep well back from the cliff edge, and hold your phone with both hands so the horizon stays level.
text.geographic_location: Karaalioğlu Park is a coastal park in Antalya, on the clifftop above the sea.
text.directions_text: No tram or train stop is listed for this spot, so go by taxi or hired scooter and ask for Hıdırlık Kulesi in Antalya. The park itself is about 200 m to the south-east. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) for the tower and the sweep of coastline together. Switch to the default lens (1x) for a calmer, less stretched view. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out boats or a stretch of cliff.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand at Hıdırlık Kulesi (cliff edge beside the tower, at the park's western end). The Hıdırlık Tower in the foreground with the sea and coastline behind it, giving a wide panorama that frames the park's cliff edge. The park stretches away to the south-east.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Switch on gridlines and place the horizon on the upper or lower line, with the tower on a side line. Keep the tower and the cliff edge in the frame, so the picture shows the park's setting. For an alternative, try the sea-facing terrace (Karaalioğlu Parkı Seyir Terası) for the bay and harbour.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the sea or sky to focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the sky keeps its colour. Try panorama mode for the full sweep of coast, moving slowly and keeping the phone level.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Late afternoon usually gives softer light on the water and the tower. Midday sun can flatten the colours and make the sea glare.

text.access_note: Access to the park and the tower's entry rules were not confirmed, so check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: Hıdırlık Tower is Roman-era (entry fee not confirmed).
Late afternoon usually gives softer light on the sea and the tower than midday.
Midday sun can cause glare on the water.

name: Hıdırlık Tower
label: Hıdırlık Tower
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Karaalioğlu Parkı' (2 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Karaalioğlu Parkı' (way/110321827): edge nearest the subject (673 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/110321832: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Hıdırlık Tower' (35 m across).
notes: Roman tower on the cliff edge above the sea.

text.description:
Hıdırlık Tower is a compact, tawny-stone tower on the edge of Antalya's old town, Kaleiçi, right where it meets Karaalioğlu Park. It is about 14 metres high: a round tower sitting on a square base. That simple shape, plus the warm stone, makes it easy to photograph against sky and sea. It is believed to have been built by the Romans in the second century CE, first on a square plan and later reshaped into a round tower. Later it served as a Byzantine military outpost and has also been used as a fortification and a lighthouse. Parts of the upper section show repairs from the Seljuk and Ottoman periods. The name Hıdırlık refers to a place where the spring festival Hıdırellez is celebrated.

The best picture here is the tower with the sea and coast behind it, taken from the seaward edge of Karaalioğlu Park, where the cliff-top is more open than the tower's own side. Around sunset the light reflects off the water, which adds colour to the stone. Stand back far enough to fit the whole tower with its base, and keep the sea in the frame so the tower has some context. If you also want a close-up of the stonework, walk to the tower's own side, where the eastern doorway is. Whether you can go inside or climb the tower is described differently in different places, so check the official site before you go.
text.geographic_location: Hıdırlık Tower stands in central Antalya, at the southern edge of the old town (Kaleiçi), where it meets Karaalioğlu Park above the sea.
text.directions_text: Start from Kaleiçi, the old town, and walk towards its southern edge, where the old town meets Karaalioğlu Park; the tower is the stone landmark there. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) to get the tower, sea and coast in one frame. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) only if you are close and want the whole tower in the picture. Use telephoto (2x or more, depending on your phone) for a tighter shot of the stone against the water.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Karaalioğlu Parkı (seaward edge of the park, next to the tower). The tower seen from the park's cliff-top edge, with the sea and the coast behind it.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Put the tower to one side and let the sea and coastline fill the rest of the frame. Turn on gridlines so the tower stands straight and the horizon is level. For the classic stone-in-front-of-the-sea view of the tower itself, walk round to the tower's own side as an alternative.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the tower to set focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the sky or the sea is bright, so the stone keeps its colour. Keep the phone steady against a railing or your elbow if you shoot at dusk.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Sunset, when the light reflects off the water behind the tower.

text.access_note: The park edge and the area around the tower are public space, but opening arrangements at the tower may change after restoration, so check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: The ultra-wide lens can make the tower's vertical lines lean if you tilt the phone upwards when close to it.
The park edge may be busier around sunset.

name: Antalya Clock Tower
label: Clock Tower
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Cumhuriyet Meydanı' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Cumhuriyet Meydanı' (way/79234506): middle (151 m across).
pin_note: Position from OSM W431455145 (Clock Tower): kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.
notes: Ottoman clock tower on Kale Kapısı square.

text.description:
The Antalya Clock Tower stands in Cumhuriyet Meydanı, and it is a popular, photogenic landmark, especially when lit at night. It is a tall, narrow stone tower, so it stands out well against the sky and against the older buildings around it. Restoration work on the dome and stone cleaning has been done, so the stone looks lighter than in older photos. Don't be surprised if it looks paler than the pictures you may have seen.

The best way to see the whole tower is to cross the square and stand on the far side, about 30 metres back. From there you can fit every face of the tower into the frame, with the old city-wall silhouette and some old arcade arches at one edge. That gives the photo a sense of place rather than just a tower on its own.

The square is busy with visitors at peak times. Overhead cables and the taxi rank can creep into the frame, so take a moment to move a few steps left or right until they are out of the way. The tower is also lit up after dark, which makes it a clear focal point for a night shot. If the square is too crowded, Cumhuriyet Caddesi gives a wider street-level view of the tower with the old-town buildings around it. Take a few frames from each position and choose later.
text.geographic_location: In Cumhuriyet Meydanı, in central Antalya.
text.directions_text: Head for Cumhuriyet Meydanı in central Antalya, the square where the tower stands. Once there, cross to the side opposite the tower and walk back about 30 metres from it. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) from the far side of the square so the whole tower fits. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) only if you are closer and the tower won't fit, and use telephoto (2x or more) to crop out cables or taxis.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Cumhuriyet Meydanı (far side of the square, about 30 m back from the tower). The whole tower with the old city-wall silhouette and old arcade arches at one edge of the frame. As an alternative, Cumhuriyet Caddesi gives a wider street-level view.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line the tower up with a vertical line so it doesn't lean. Leave a little sky above the dome and place the arcade arches at one edge of the frame. Shuffle left or right to keep cables and the taxi rank out of the shot. Cumhuriyet Caddesi is a good second position if you want more of the surrounding square.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the tower to focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the sky stays blue and the stone doesn't wash out. After dark, use night mode and hold the phone firmly against your body or a solid surface until it finishes.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: After dark, when the tower is lit up and stands out clearly as a focal point.

text.access_note: The viewpoint is free. Check the official site before you go if you want to know about any access restrictions.
claims_not_in_sources: Holding the phone against your body or a solid surface helps keep night shots steady.

name: Yivli Minaret Mosque
label: Yivli Minaret
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Cumhuriyet Meydanı' (2 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Cumhuriyet Meydanı' (way/79234506): middle (151 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/154761774: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Yivli Minaret Mosque' (38 m across).
notes: Symbol of Antalya, a 13th-century fluted minaret.

text.description:
The Yivli Minaret Mosque (Yivli Minare Camii) sits in Kaleiçi, Antalya's old town, and its tall fluted brick tower is the shape most people link with the city. The shaft is made of red brick, rises from a heavy square stone base and is divided into eight fluted sections. Traces of the turquoise and dark blue tiles that once covered it can still be seen. The tower is about 38 metres high.

The first mosque here dates to around 1230, after the Seljuk takeover of the city. It was rebuilt in 1373, and the prayer hall now has six domes. Restoration finished in 2010 and uncovered old water channels under the building, which can be seen through a glass section of floor.

It photographs well because the brick tower stands out against the sky and the old-town entrance gives it a good setting. The easiest view of the whole tower is from Cumhuriyet Meydanı, where the square lies in front and the minaret rises above the way into Kaleiçi. Stand back far enough to fit the base and the top in one shot. For a different angle, try the square beside the minaret (called Yivli Minaret Square in one guide), or look up the shaft from the courtyard of the complex. The mosque is still used for worship, so be quiet and considerate, and avoid photographing during prayer times.
text.geographic_location: In Kaleiçi, the old town of Antalya, on Cumhuriyet Street close to Kalekapısı Square; some guides place it just south of Cumhuriyet Meydanı (Republic Square).
text.directions_text: No tram or railway stops are listed for this spot, but the area can be reached on foot. Head for Cumhuriyet Meydanı at the entrance to Kaleiçi. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) to fit the whole minaret and some of the square in the frame. Switch to the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the brick flutes and the fragments of blue tile near the top. In the courtyard, where you are close to the base, the ultra-wide (0.5x) helps you look up the full shaft.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Cumhuriyet Meydanı (south of the square, at the entrance to Kaleiçi). The full fluted brick minaret rising above the entrance to the old town, with the square in the foreground.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line the tower up with a vertical line so it stands straight. Leave a little space above the top and include some of the square at the bottom for depth. For an alternative, try the square beside the minaret (called Yivli Minaret Square in one guide) for the minaret seen across it, or the courtyard of the complex for a low angle looking up the shaft.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the brick, not the sky, to set focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the sky does not wash out. Keep your phone upright and avoid tilting it back, which makes the tower lean. Ask permission before photographing inside the mosque.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Morning or late afternoon, when the square is quieter and cooler than at midday, especially in summer.

text.access_note: The minaret can be seen from the open square, but the mosque is an active place of worship, so avoid prayer times and ask before taking photos inside.

name: Murat Pasha Mosque
label: Murat Pasha Mosque
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Murat Paşa Camii' (2 web pages); placed at our map tiles: 'Tekeli Mehmet Paşa Camii' (pois); moved 15 m off buildings.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/91735627: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Muratpaşa Camii' (34 m across).

text.description:
Murat Paşa Camii is an Ottoman mosque in the Muratpaşa district of Antalya. It was commissioned in 1570 by Murat Pasha of Karaman. What you'll want to photograph is the outside: a large central dome sits on a ten-sided drum, with a slender minaret beside it. The calm, solid shape of the building means a straight-on view works well. The porch at the front has three domes on pointed arches of coloured stone, held up by four round columns. That is a good detail for a second, closer shot. Inside, bands of calligraphy run around the walls, and the marble pulpit has carved reliefs. Both are worth a look if you visit as a guest.

The walk to the mosque is a separate step: head about 600 m north-west. The forecourt at the front of the mosque is the place to go for the frontal view, where the dome, its drum and the minaret should all fit in one frame, though the exact standing point there is not well documented. For a second angle, walk along Milli Egemenlik Caddesi as you approach. Seen from the avenue, the minaret and dome rise above the street, which gives a more relaxed, everyday scene. Keep the phone level so the minaret stays upright, and leave a little space around the dome rather than cropping tight. If you go in, dress modestly (a head covering is recommended for women), keep quiet and avoid flash. Don't photograph people who are praying.
text.geographic_location: Murat Paşa Camii is in the Muratpaşa district of Antalya, outside the old walls of the historic centre. Check the map for the exact frontage before you set off.
text.directions_text: If you come along Milli Egemenlik Caddesi, the minaret and dome show above the street as you get closer. Once you reach the front of the mosque, use the forecourt for the frontal view. Check the map for the exact frontage, because the street names around the mosque vary between guides. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the frontal view of dome, drum and minaret. Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) only if the forecourt is too tight to fit the whole building in. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the three-domed porch or the top of the minaret.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject (front exterior, from the forecourt across the street). The mosque's large central dome, its ten-sided drum and the minaret in one frontal view. The exact standing point on the forecourt is not well documented, so use the map and your own eye to find where the whole building fits.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Switch on the gridlines and line the minaret up with a vertical line so it doesn't lean. Leave a little sky above the dome. For a second shot, take the mosque from Milli Egemenlik Caddesi as you approach, with the minaret and dome rising above the street. Then zoom in on the porch's coloured-stone arches.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the walls to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly if the sky is bright, so the dome keeps its detail. If you take photos inside, don't use flash and keep your phone quiet.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Choose a time when the front is lit rather than in shadow, and when few people are in the shot. Avoid prayer times, and don't point your phone at worshippers.

text.access_note: This is a working place of worship: dress modestly (a head covering is recommended for women) and take photos quietly inside, without flash.
claims_not_in_sources: The three-domed porch and coloured-stone arches make a good close-up with a telephoto lens.
The front of the mosque photographs better when lit by the sun than when in shade, and quieter times mean fewer people in the frame.
The forecourt may be too tight for the whole building at 1x, so the ultra-wide may help.
The exact standing point on the forecourt for the frontal view is not well documented.

name: Kesik Minaret Mosque
label: Kesik Minaret
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Hesapçı Sokak' (3 web pages); placed at the stretch of Hesapçı Sokak nearest the subject (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from OSM W431519181 (Kesik Minare): kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.
notes: Ruined Byzantine church turned mosque with a broken minaret.

text.description:
Kesik Minare, the "Cut Minaret", is a mosque in the Kaleiçi old town, with a fenced ruin beside the minaret. The minaret is what draws the eye. Its cone and balcony were restored around 2019, and the mosque reopened in 2021, so older photos online may show a truncated top that no longer matches what you will see. The ruins around it are fenced off and the mosque is in use, so you photograph it from the lane rather than from inside the site.

The best picture here is a street picture. From Hesapçı Sokak, on the stretch between Hadrian's Gate and the mosque, you look along a narrow lane with the minaret at the far end and traditional Kaleiçi houses on either side. The walls lead the eye straight to the tower, which gives a phone photo depth without any fuss. If you want a second angle, walk to Cami Sokak. From the corner there the minaret rises directly above the ruin and the surrounding rooftops, and you can shoot it straight on.

Keep the minaret upright in the frame and leave a little space above it so the top is not cut off. Be patient: the lane is narrow, and people walking through will often spoil a clear shot, so wait for a gap. Visit outside prayer times, and be respectful when photographing, especially if people are going in or out of the mosque.
text.geographic_location: In the Kaleiçi old town of Antalya, on the lane that runs past the mosque from Hadrian's Gate. The mosque stands among the old houses of the district.
text.directions_text: There are no stations or tram stops nearby, so head for Kaleiçi old town on foot and walk in through Hadrian's Gate. Follow Hesapçı Sokak towards the mosque. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) to show the lane and the houses leading to the minaret. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) if the lane feels too tight. Use telephoto (2x or more, depending on your phone) to bring the minaret closer without moving into the road.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Hesapçı Sokak (Stretch between Hadrian's Gate and the mosque, looking toward the minaret). The truncated minaret framed at the far end of the narrow old-town lane, with traditional Kaleiçi houses around it. The minaret is to the east. For the alternative view, go to Cami Sokak and shoot from the corner, where the minaret rises directly above the ruin and the rooftops.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Hold the phone upright and turn on the gridlines. Place the minaret on a vertical grid line and let the house walls on each side form a frame. Keep the phone level so the walls do not lean inwards. Take a second shot from Cami Sokak, looking straight at the minaret above the ruin.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the minaret to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the sky keeps its colour and the stone does not wash out. Shaded lanes next to bright sky can confuse the phone, so check the screen before you take the shot.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Weekday mornings tend to be quieter, which helps in such a narrow lane.

text.access_note: The mosque is in use and the ruins around it are fenced, so enjoy the view from the street. If you plan to enter, go outside prayer times and be respectful.
claims_not_in_sources: The lane is narrow enough that passers-by can easily get into the frame, so waiting for a gap helps.
Visitors to an active mosque are usually expected to dress modestly.
Shaded lanes with bright sky above can confuse a phone's exposure.

name: Tekeli Mehmet Pasha Mosque
label: Tekeli Mehmet Pasha
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Tekeli Mehmet Paşa Camii' (2 web pages); placed at at the subject (split pin).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/91728307: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Tekeli Mehmet Paşa Camii' (50 m across).
notes: Ottoman mosque on the edge of Kaleiçi.

text.description: Tekeli Mehmet Pasha Mosque is a 17th-century Ottoman mosque in Antalya, built in the Kalekapisi district and counted among the most important Ottoman mosques in the city. It takes its name from Lala Mehmed Pasa. It photographs well because the shapes are so clear. The main dome rises on a high rim and is held by three semi-domes to the east, west and south, with three domes along the northern side. The northern façade is the classic view. Its pointed window arches (lunettes) carry tiled panels with Koranic verses in taliq script, which make a good close-up. The phone icon on the map is at the mosque itself. The classic north view is taken from the north side of the building, about 20 m north of its centre, looking at that façade with the main dome rising behind the northern domes. The calm grounds around the building also work as a backdrop for people. Take one wide shot to show the whole group of domes, then a closer shot of the tiled panels and arches. Photography inside is allowed, but without flash and never during prayer. Check locally for any restoration work before you go, as scaffolding can spoil the view.
text.geographic_location: In the Kalekapisi area of Antalya's old centre, right behind the Antalya clock tower at the entrance to Kaleiçi.
text.directions_text: Head for the Antalya clock tower at the entrance to Kaleiçi; the mosque stands right behind it. No tram or railway stop is listed for this spot, so use the clock tower as your landmark and walk the short distance from there. Once there, the phone icon on the map is at the mosque itself; walk to its north side for the postcard view. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the head-on view of the northern façade. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if you cannot step back far enough to fit all the domes in. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the tiled panels and window arches.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and use them to keep the façade level. Place the main dome near the centre and let the other domes spread out on either side. Keep your phone upright so the dome rim does not lean. A second option is to take in the exterior and the calm grounds around it, with the mosque as the backdrop for a person or group.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the façade to set focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the sky is bright so the dome keeps its detail. Do not use flash or take photos while prayer is under way.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Choose a time when the façade is evenly lit and shoot away from the sun. Early morning or late afternoon is usually quieter and kinder to the stonework.

text.access_note: This is a working place of worship; photography inside is allowed without flash and not during prayer, and it is worth checking locally before you go in case of restoration works.

name: Kaleiçi Old Harbour
label: Old Harbour
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Hıdırlık Kulesi' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Hıdırlık Kulesi' (way/110321832): middle (35 m across); moved 10 m off buildings.
pin_note: Position from Wikidata Q5994531: kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.
notes: Historic Roman harbour below the cliffs with boat trips.

text.description:
Kaleiçi Old Harbour is the small basin at the foot of Antalya's old town, where the ancient port has become a modern yacht marina. Boats sit in calm water, with the old walls and cliffs behind them and red-tiled houses stacked up the slope. That layering of water, stone and rooftops is why it photographs so well. It also reads clearly on a small phone screen.

The harbour is the original heart of the city. Kaleiçi means "Inner Castle", and the district is enclosed by a double ring of walls. It still has around 3,000 traditional houses with red-tiled roofs, and narrow alleys run uphill from the water. A few traces of the ancient harbour breakwater survive, which makes the setting more than just a pretty marina.

It is about 31 m north of the harbour, so you look south across the basin. For a higher view, Hıdırlık Kulesi is a separate, recommended elevated viewpoint. This Roman-era tower is open to the air and reached on foot from Karaalioğlu Park. From its western side you look over the Kaleiçi rooftops, the old harbour and the Mediterranean, and before sunset the sun drops over the water. If the tower is busy or you want a closer view, Keçili Parkı looks down on the boats, and Kaleiçi Yat Limanı gives a view of the whole basin with reflections.

Take a few wide shots first, then step in on the details: masts, rooftops and the line of the walls.
text.geographic_location: The harbour is in Kaleiçi, the historic centre of Antalya, on the Mediterranean coast. It sits at the foot of the old town, below the walls and the red-tiled houses.
text.directions_text: No Underground, tram or train stops are listed for this spot, so the area is best reached on foot within the Kaleiçi old town in central Antalya. The harbour lies 31 m to the south. If you want an optional elevated view instead, Hıdırlık Kulesi is a separate viewpoint, reached on foot from Karaalioğlu Park. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for a natural view of the harbour and rooftops. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if you want more of the sky and sea. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out boats, masts or a stretch of wall.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand at Hıdırlık Kulesi (western side of the tower). A wide panorama of the Kaleiçi rooftops, the old harbour and the Mediterranean, with the sun setting over the water.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and put the horizon on the upper or lower line, so the picture is mostly rooftops and water or mostly sky. Keep the red roofs in the foreground and let the harbour sit in the middle distance. Try one wide shot and one tighter telephoto shot of the boats. If you prefer a lower view, Keçili Parkı and the harbour's edge are good alternatives.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the sea or the sky to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the sunset colours don't wash out. Panorama mode can suit the sweep of rooftops and coast. Pan slowly and hold the phone level.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Golden hour before sunset, when the sun sets over the water. If you go up to Hıdırlık Kulesi instead, its western side is recommended for the sunset light.

text.access_note: Hıdırlık Kulesi is a public open-air tower, but check the official site before you go in case access has changed.
